For three weeks I stayed off everything after the pile-on, and it helped. But when I finally went back, I did it differently. I kept only a small circle of people I actually know. I decided to open messages twice a day, at one and at eight, and never in bed. I set a timer on the phone that stops me after thirty minutes.

The part I was most reluctant about was talking to Aparna, the counsellor at my college. I expected to be told I'd overreacted. Instead she asked what I needed to feel safe, and we wrote it down together. The platform is not the enemy. I just needed a healthier way to be there, and I'm still working on it. Baljeet

Counselling note, week 7. Written by Elizabeth, campus counsellor.
Vidya came back today to talk about returning online. It has been five weeks since the pile-on over her poetry reading clip, and she deleted the apps the night it started.
She arrived with a plan written in her notebook, which I noticed first. A new account, open only to about thirty people she knows offline. Messages checked twice a day, after lunch and at seven, with the app off otherwise. No reading comments on anything public.
She said the first week back had gone badly: she had checked the phone every few minutes and felt her chest tighten. "That's when I made the times," she said. This week she had stuck to them five days out of seven.
What I did next: we agreed to keep meeting every Thursday for a month, and I suggested she tell me if the old habit comes back.

qa.q: At what times does Vidya check her messages?
qa.a: She checks them twice a day, after lunch and at seven.

qa.q: How was Vidya feeling in her first week back, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt anxious and on edge, checking the phone every few minutes and noticing her chest tighten.

qa.q: What else could Vidya add to her routine if the old habit returns?
qa.a: She could ask a close friend to check in on the days she struggles, so support is not only in the Thursday meetings.

qa.q: How does Vidya's return look to the counsellor?
qa.a: The counsellor notices the written plan first and sees steady progress, five days out of seven, and keeps meeting weekly to support it.

grounding: Shows the student returning after a pile-on with a smaller circle, set checking times and regular sessions with a counsellor.

Sunday, 9 p.m.
Six weeks since it happened. Today I reinstalled the app for the first time.
I made a new account and only added people I'd actually trust with my phone number: Devika, my cousins, a few from class. Twenty-two people. It feels tiny and safe.
The rules are on a sticky note on my mirror: messages at 1 and at 8, fifteen minutes each. Nothing after 9. I set a timer for tonight's check and it rang before I'd finished scrolling, which was a shock. I closed it anyway.
Saw the counsellor again on Friday. We talked about how my hands still shake when a notification sound plays, even on other apps. She said that's normal after what happened and we'd work on it.
Devika sent me a silly photo of her dog within a minute of me joining. I laughed out loud.
Tanuja

How does Tanuja feel about returning to the app?

qa.a: Tanuja could keep the phone outside the bedroom after nine, so the rule does not depend only on willpower late at night.

qa.a: Devika is likely glad and relieved, sending a silly dog photo within a minute to welcome Tanuja back.
